entities.name: Bagrat VI of Georgia
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Bagrat VI, a pivotal figure in the 15th-century fragmentation of the unified Kingdom of Georgia, emerged from the Imeretian branch of the Bagrationi dynasty, ultimately reigning as King of Imereti from 1463 and as King of Georgia from 1466 until his death in 1478. His reign encapsulates a period of intense internal strife, where the central authority of the Georgian crown irrevocably collapsed, giving way to the formation of independent kingdoms and principalities. Bagrat's ascendance was a direct challenge to the reigning Bagrationi monarchs, particularly George VIII and later Constantine II, exacerbating the centrifugal forces that were tearing Georgia apart.

His path to power was marked by military conflict and political maneuvering. Initially, as a duke and then a rebel, Bagrat exploited the discontent of western Georgian nobility against King George VIII. Following his victory at the decisive Battle of Chikhory in 1463 against George VIII's forces, Bagrat declared himself King of Imereti, effectively establishing an independent kingdom in western Georgia. Three years later, in 1466, he capitalized on the capture of King George VIII by the atabeg of Samtskhe to seize the capital, Tbilisi, and proclaim himself King of all Georgia. His rule was, however, continuously contested by George VIII (who subsequently became King of Kakheti) and Prince Constantine, who eventually became King Constantine II of Kartli, leading to further civil war.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Bagrat VI's reign marked the definitive end of a unified Georgian kingdom, permanently splitting it into three separate entities and several principalities. This fragmentation led to centuries of internal weakness and increased vulnerability to foreign powers, fundamentally reshaping the region's political destiny.
